strengths: The paper identifies a useful problem: explanations based on selected, interpretable macro-level features can suffer from confounding even when the predictor is a deterministic function of its pixel inputs. This connection should interest researchers in causal discovery, interpretability, and model auditing.

Under the stated causal assumptions, using FCI with background knowledge that predictions cannot cause image content is a principled approach. Representing ambiguity through PAGs is valuable and avoids requiring an unjustifiably complete causal graph.

The shape simulation provides an accessible illustration of the intended causal-versus-confounded distinction. The two image applications make the workflow concrete, and Sections 7.2–7.3 usefully discuss identifiability, background knowledge, and the difficulty of obtaining interpretable features.
weaknesses: Necessary: Correct the interpretation of the graph summaries in Sections 6.3–6.4 and Figures 9–10. Absence of an edge adjacent to the prediction does not establish absence of a causal effect: a feature can act through another observed feature. Figure 10 itself contains the possibly causal path Cardiomegaly o→ Atelectasis → prediction. Furthermore, pooling directed and partially directed edge frequencies obscures the distinction between identified ancestry and unresolved confounding; a consistently selected o→ edge need not represent a true cause. Report these distinctions separately and assess ancestral paths before making claims of causal irrelevance.

Necessary: Repair Example 1 and Appendix A. The quantities labeled as valid causal adjustment average remaining variables over their observational marginals, although interventions on Z2 or Z3 can change their descendant Z1. They therefore do not generally equal the corresponding macro-level interventional expectations. Appendix A.2 also leaves the supposedly omitted Z3 fixed inside the prediction function and changes the baseline, rather than deriving an adjustment estimator using only observed variables. Consequently, the displayed zero-versus-nonzero comparison does not establish the claimed confounding failure as written. Define the intervention game precisely and rederive the example, or remove it.

Necessary: Address selection in the X-ray experiment. Section 6.1 selects pneumonia cases and controls specifically having 'no findings,' so inclusion depends on both diagnosis and the explanatory findings. This can introduce selection-induced associations, whereas Section 3 dismisses selection bias and the subsequent edge interpretations assume it absent. FCI's ability to accommodate latent confounding does not by itself justify those interpretations under selection. Explicitly model the sampling mechanism and its implications, change the analysis design, or narrow the clinical causal conclusions.

Necessary: Better support or narrow the empirical causal claims. Clinical plausibility and bootstrap stability do not validate causal correctness. The chi-square conditional-independence tests also face potentially severe sparsity with 26 multilevel bird attributes and only 240 X-rays, without reported contingency-count diagnostics or calibration. Specify the exact samples used for discovery, establish the adequacy of the tests and conditioning restrictions, and provide evidence for reliable causal discrimination. Alternatively, consistently present the real-data graphs as exploratory implications of the assumptions rather than established determinants of model behavior.

Optional: The LIME/SHAP comparison illustrates different explanatory resolutions, but it does not isolate the benefit of causal discovery because the proposed method receives additional human annotations. A comparison using the same macro-level features would strengthen comparative claims. Additional simulation repetitions and sample-size sensitivity analyses would also help characterize practical reliability; a new method or state-of-the-art predictive performance is not required.
